title: Tested in the Wilderness, Rejected at Nazareth

verses.text: Then Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness,
where for forty days He was tempted by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they had ended, He was hungry.
The devil said to Him, "If You are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread."
But Jesus answered, "It is written: 'Man shall not live on bread alone.'"
Then the devil led Him up to a high place and showed Him in an instant all the kingdoms of the world.
"I will give You authority over all these kingdoms and all their glory," he said. "For it has been relinquished to me, and I can give it to anyone I wish.
So if You worship me, it will all be Yours."
But Jesus answered, "It is written: 'Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.'"
Then the devil led Him to Jerusalem and set Him on the pinnacle of the temple. "If You are the Son of God," he said, "throw Yourself down from here.
For it is written: 'He will command His angels concerning You to guard You carefully,
and they will lift You up in their hands, so that You will not strike Your foot against a stone.'"
But Jesus answered, "It also says, 'Do not put the Lord your God to the test.'"
When the devil had finished every temptation, he left Him until an opportune time.
Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, and the news about Him spread throughout the surrounding region.
He taught in their synagogues and was glorified by everyone.
Then Jesus came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up. As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath. And when He stood up to read,
the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to Him. Unrolling it, He found the place where it was written:

"The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to release the oppressed,
to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor."
Then He rolled up the scroll, returned it to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on Him,
and He began by saying, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing."
All spoke well of Him and marveled at the gracious words that came from His lips. "Isn't this the son of Joseph?" they asked.
Jesus said to them, "Surely you will quote this proverb to Me: 'Physician, heal yourself! Do here in Your hometown what we have heard that You did in Capernaum.'"
Then He added, "Truly I tell you, no prophet is accepted in his hometown.
But I tell you truthfully that there were many widows in Israel in the time of Elijah, when the sky was shut for three and a half years and great famine swept over all the land.
Yet Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon.
And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet. Yet not one of them was cleansed—only Naaman the Syrian."
On hearing this, all the people in the synagogue were enraged.
They got up, drove Him out of the town, and led Him to the brow of the hill on which the town was built, in order to throw Him over the cliff.
But Jesus passed through the crowd and went on His way.
Then He went down to Capernaum, a town in Galilee, and on the Sabbath He began to teach the people.
They were astonished at His teaching, because His message had authority.
In the synagogue there was a man possessed by the spirit of an unclean demon. He cried out in a loud voice,
"Ha! What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us? I know who You are—the Holy One of God!"
But Jesus rebuked the demon. "Be silent!" He said. "Come out of him!" At this, the demon threw the man down before them all and came out without harming him.
All the people were overcome with amazement and asked one another, "What is this message? With authority and power He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!"
And the news about Jesus spread throughout the surrounding region.
After Jesus had left the synagogue, He went to the home of Simon, whose mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever. So they appealed to Jesus on her behalf,
and He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. And she got up at once and began to serve them.
At sunset, all who were ill with various diseases were brought to Jesus, and laying His hands on each one, He healed them.
Demons also came out of many people, shouting, "You are the Son of God!" But He rebuked the demons and would not allow them to speak, because they knew He was the Christ.
At daybreak, Jesus went out to a solitary place, and the crowds were looking for Him. They came to Him and tried to keep Him from leaving.
But Jesus told them, "I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is why I was sent."
And He continued to preach in the synagogues of Judea.

context.author: Traditionally Luke, a Gentile physician and traveling companion of the apostle Paul, who also wrote the book of Acts
context.genre: Historical narrative — three linked scenes that move Jesus from private testing in the wilderness to public proclamation in Nazareth and Capernaum
context.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile Greek-speaking readership
context.setting: The chapter begins in the barren wilderness of Judea, then moves to Nazareth, a small hill village in lower Galilee, and finally to Capernaum, a fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee. Excavators at Capernaum have found a limestone synagogue built on top of an earlier basalt foundation, likely the type of building Jesus taught in.
context.custom: In a synagogue service the reader stood to read from the scroll, and the one who taught sat down, which is why Luke notes that Jesus sat before speaking. The "year of the Lord's favor" echoes the Jubilee of Leviticus 25, when debts were canceled, slaves freed, and land returned to its families. Luke's word for Peter's mother-in-law's "high fever" is a medical term, a detail often connected to Luke being a physician.
context.timelineImmediate: The chapter follows straight from Jesus' baptism and genealogy in chapter 3 and carries Him from forty days of fasting to the beginning of His public work in Galilee. Luke's order of the three temptations (bread, kingdoms, temple) differs from Matthew's, which puts the temple second and the kingdoms last. Luke also places the Nazareth visit at the start of the ministry, and readers differ on whether Matthew 13 and Mark 6 describe the same visit or a later one.
context.timelineBible: Jesus answers each temptation from Deuteronomy (8:3, 6:13, 6:16), the same book that recounts Israel's forty years of testing in the wilderness, so He meets in forty days the kind of test Israel failed. At Nazareth He reads Isaiah 61:1-2 and stops mid-sentence, leaving off "the day of vengeance of our God," and then points to Elijah and Elisha helping outsiders.
context.sparkNotes: Full of the Spirit, Jesus is led into the wilderness, where after forty days of fasting the devil tests Him three times: turn stones to bread, take the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship, and throw Himself from the temple. Each time Jesus answers with Scripture, and the devil leaves until a more opportune time. In Nazareth He reads Isaiah's promise of good news to the poor and announces it is fulfilled that day, but when He reminds the crowd that God sent Elijah and Elisha to outsiders, the hometown congregation tries to throw Him off a cliff. In Capernaum He teaches with authority, drives out an unclean spirit, heals Peter's mother-in-law and many others at sunset, and tells the crowds He must preach the kingdom in other towns too.

translation.meaning: To test or put to the proof. The same verb is used for the devil's attempt to trip Jesus here and for people testing God, as in Jesus' answer in verse 12. The Greek word holds both "test" and "tempt," and the context decides which.
To anoint with oil, the act that set apart kings, priests, and prophets. It is the verb behind the title "Christ" (Anointed One), so Jesus' reading of Isaiah is also a statement of who He is.

The right or power to act. It appears on the devil's lips in verse 6, where he claims authority over the kingdoms, and again in verses 32 and 36, where the crowd sees Jesus' own authority in His teaching and over unclean spirits.

otBackground.note: "Man shall not live on bread alone" — Jesus' first answer, spoken to Israel after its time in the wilderness.
Worship God only, and do not test Him — Jesus' second and third answers.
The anointed one who brings good news to the poor, the passage Jesus reads at Nazareth.
The Jubilee year of release behind the phrase "the year of the Lord's favor."
Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, and Elisha and Naaman — the two outsiders Jesus names in verses 25-27.

commentary.note: Henry observes that being led into the wilderness gave the tempter an advantage, since Jesus was alone, with no one by whose prayers and advice He might be helped. "He who knew his own strength might give Satan advantage; but we may not, who know our own weakness." He also notes that Satan found nothing in Christ for his "fiery darts to fasten upon," and that Christ conquered "not for himself only, but for us also."

Ryle points out that the verb for "led" is the same one used of the Spirit's guidance of believers, so Jesus "did not seek conflict with the devil, but was 'led' to it." He draws two warnings from the scene: that the devil can quote Scripture when it suits his purpose, and that the acts he suggests are often trifling in appearance while the principle behind them is rebellion against God. At Nazareth, he says, the claim that God had favored outsiders "wounded their pride and self-conceit."

Guzik reads "the acceptable year of the Lord" as the Old Testament Jubilee, when slaves were set free, debts canceled, and everything given a new start, so Jesus' announcement at Nazareth is that the Jubilee has arrived in His own person. On the first temptation, he stresses that Jesus reminded Satan that "every word of God is more important than the very bread we eat."

overview.summary: Full of the Spirit, Jesus resists three temptations in the wilderness by answering with Scripture. In Nazareth He reads Isaiah's promise of good news and is rejected by His hometown. In Capernaum He teaches with authority, drives out a demon, and heals many.

history.t: Many Jews longed for an anointed deliverer to free them from foreign rule.
It sat on a busy trade route near the border of Herod Antipas' territory.

customs.t: A reader stood to read, and the teacher sat down to speak, as Jesus does here.
The "year of the Lord's favor" echoes Jubilee, when debts were erased and slaves freed.

archaeology.t: A limestone synagogue sits on older basalt walls from the first-century town.
The complete Isaiah scroll found at Qumran shows what a scroll like His looked like.

overview.discussion: Each temptation offered something good by the wrong means. How do you tell a good thing from a shortcut?
